## (1) First message

```text
gauntlet: question
These claims come from the gather draft. I have not re-read primary code in this response, so I treat each as unverified until the code confirms it.

The draft says the reports page renders a table with no export action today. It says the table's column definitions and the existing CSV serializer already support export, and src/export/csv.ts already reuses those column definitions. The design depends on that reuse, so I will confirm it in src/export/csv.ts and the table's column definitions before the design round. The draft also says paging supports the 10k-row target. That is the claim behind "under 60s", and it has an implicit dependency: a 10k-row report fixture or dataset to time the export against. The draft names no such fixture and no lookup for one, so that dependency is unverified. I am carrying it as an open question rather than stopping on it.

The framing holds: checked the draft's claim that src/export/csv.ts reuses the table column definitions, the paging path behind the 10k-row target, and the 10k-row timing dependency. That dependency is unverified, and no cited case shows the ask is misdiagnosed, wrong-sized, or already solved.

The ticket groups one acceptance row under "phase 2": "Exports are emailed to the requesting user." That heading matches neither this repo (acme/widgets, from the overrides' Issue tracker) nor any known member. It reads as a delivery phase, not a repo. Which repo owns that row?
A) this repo
B) elsewhere: phase 2
C) repair the ticket - /skill:shape-ticket acme/widgets#77
```

## (2) Approaches message

*Assumes the "phase 2" answer keeps emailing out of this repo's scope (B or C). If the answer is A, emailing enters scope and this approach set changes.*

Recorded answers adopted: the button sits beside the report title, and the export uses the visible table columns in table order.

One dependency is still open. The 10k-row timing check needs a 10k-row report fixture or dataset. The draft names none, and I have done no lookup in this response. Until one is found, the "under 60s" row's test is an open question and not a confirmed test.

**Recommended: reuse-only. Add a button that drives the existing serializer over the existing paging.**
The axis between the approaches is where rows are gathered and serialized: on the client from paged reads, or in a new server path.

This approach adds an Export CSV button beside the report title. The button walks the report through the existing paging, passes the visible column definitions in table order to src/export/csv.ts, and downloads the result. No new serializer, endpoint, or column list is created.

Trade-off: the whole 10k-row CSV is assembled in the browser. That is fine if the paging really does meet the draft's 10k-row claim. Rows the user has filtered client-side would need care to match "every column shown."

Removes: none
Adds: Export CSV button in the reports page header; click handler that pages through the report and calls src/export/csv.ts with the visible column definitions; test for column parity and order; 10k-row timing test (fixture pending)
Pattern: follows src/export/csv.ts's existing reuse of the table column definitions, keeping one column contract for display and export.

**Alternative: a server-side streaming export endpoint.**
A new endpoint pages through the report on the server and streams CSV rows back. The browser no longer holds 10k rows, which is safer if client memory or paging round-trips threaten the 60s target.

Trade-off: the server needs its own copy of the visible-column contract. That means passing the column list from the client or duplicating the definitions, which is a second column path beside the one src/export/csv.ts already uses.

Removes: none
Adds: export endpoint and handler; server-side use of the serializer; request parameter carrying visible column ids; endpoint test; button wiring; 10k-row timing test (fixture pending)
Pattern: cuts across the single column contract that src/export/csv.ts shares with the table by moving column selection to a second layer.

**Not viable here: dropping the synchronous-download assumption.**
An async background export job is not viable in this scope. Its only delivery channel is the emailing row the "phase 2" question is settling, so it would pull out-of-scope work in.

What would flip the recommendation: if the paging cannot gather 10k rows within 60s in the browser once a fixture is found, the server-side streaming endpoint wins.
